reason: The sources provide enough factual details to support a compelling 45-second story with well over 10 mutually supported claims.
story: In 1985, Europe launched the Giotto spacecraft on a daring suicide mission: plunge directly into the heart of Halley's Comet at 150,000 miles per hour. Scientists estimated its survival odds anywhere from ninety percent to zero. To survive a barrage of comet dust that could act like bullets, engineers protected Giotto with a specialized Whipple shield featuring an aluminum front plate and a Kevlar rear sheet. On March 14, 1986, Giotto passed within 596 kilometers of the nucleus. Right before closest approach, it hit a wall of dust, and a one-gram particle knocked the probe wildly off-axis. Yet, despite losing its camera and temporarily dropping communications, Giotto survived. It captured the first close-up images of a comet's dark, peanut-shaped nucleus, proving comets are pristine time capsules from the birth of the solar system 4.5 billion years ago.
angle: A tiny space probe surviving a high-speed collision with 150,000 mph comet dust to snap the first-ever close-ups of Halley's nucleus.

claims.claim: The spacecraft was launched on an Ariane 1 rocket.
Giotto was named after Italian painter Giotto di Bondone.
The spacecraft approached Halley's nucleus on March 13 or 14, 1986.
Giotto passed at a distance of 596 kilometers from Halley's nucleus.
The combined speed of the spacecraft and comet during encounter was approximately 245,000 km/h or 68 km/s.
The dust shield featured a 1 mm aluminum sheet and a 12 mm Kevlar sheet.
An impact 7.6 seconds before closest approach sent the spacecraft spinning off its axis.
Giotto re-stabilized itself within 32 minutes and restored communication.
Halley's nucleus was found to be a dark, peanut-shaped body approximately 15 km long.
Giotto was later reactivated and flew by Comet Grigg–Skjellerup on July 10, 1992.
Giotto was the first spacecraft to make close-up observations of a comet nucleus.

disputed: Sources differ slightly on the exact closest approach distance calculation and whether the closest approach time was March 13 or March 14 depending on time zones (UTC vs local time). The script should state it was March 1986 and approximately 596 kilometers.
Estimates of the exact mass of the impacting particle that knocked the spacecraft spinning range from 0.1 grams to 1 gram; the script should note it was a fraction of a gram up to a gram.
